This seems quite a bit more natural, and allows more safety in the implementation. Please install the dev version and check out the new form, and let me know if you would like additional components exposed as well.

As well, you no longer have to supply a dummy local pattern input on the initial definition through mirtCAT() (I too found that annoying while testing). HTH.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: equating IRT models
messages.body_plain:
Concurrent calibration with those items listed in the invariance statement is the most straightforward and defensible way of linking/equating IRT scales.

Standard IRT equating (mean/mean Stocking Lord etc.) does not provide a model that incorporates true invariance assumptions, these weaker methods only exploit scale indeterminacy and do not constrain the model at all.

The invariance statement in the multiplegroup mirt call is pretty flexible, you can say which items are invariant, or what types of parameters, etc

see page 134 in https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/mirt/mirt.pdf

This equality constraint invariance modeling is standard and can be shown to be the strongest link (strict invariance on linking items) as for example described here:

von Davier, M, Yamamoto, K., Shin, H.-J., Chen, H., Khorramdel, L., Weeks, J., Davis, S. Kong, N.  Kandathil, M. (2019) Evaluating item response theory linking and model fit for data from PISA 2000–2012, Assessment in Education: Principles, Policy & Practice, DOI: 10.1080/0969594X.2019.1586642

and here

von Davier, M., Khorramdel, L., He, Q., Shin, H. J., & Chen, H. (2019). Developments in Psychometric Population Models for Technology-Based Large-Scale Assessments: An Overview of Challenges and Opportunities. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, 44(6), 671–705. https://doi.org/10.3102/1076998619881789

and here

von Davier, M. & von Davier, A. (2007). A Unified Approach to IRT Scale Linkage and Scale Transformations. Methodology, 3, 3, 115-124. https://econtent.hogrefe.com/ doi/abs/10.1027/1614-2241.3.3.115?journalCode=med

as well as

Xu, X. & von Davier, M. (2008). Linking with the General Diagnostic Model.  Research Report, RR-08-08. ETS: Princeton, NJ. http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/j.2333-8504.2008.tb02094.x/full

similar approaches that also allow partial invariance, just as the articles above, were described by  Glas & Jehangir, 2014, Glas & Verhelst, 1995, Yamamoto & Mazzeo, 1992, Oliveri & von Davier 2011.

messages.subject_clean: Fixed calibration - how to make mirt calibrate with MWU-MEM method
messages.body_plain:
Hi Hugo,

I finally found a few hours (and more importantly, energy) to look into the details of the paper and how to perform these fixed calibration methods with mirt. It turns out that mirt is capable of executing each of these methods right now without any modifications to the package (I was surprised by this, actually, so it looks like my previous work exposing customized density/probability functions was more useful than I initially anticipated!). See the attached R script for a demonstration. This was a fun little exercise, and much of these estimation methods could certainly be rolled into a single function and distributed in mirt. I'll consider doing this in the future if researchers actually are interested in these types of fixed calibration methods (if you know any other methods that would fall within the IRT estimation framework feel free to send those along and I'll add them to my reading/implementation list).

As an aside, my general impression of these techniques at this point is only so-so. They feel quite ad-hoc, and even the most appealing "Multiple Prior Weights Updating and Multiple EM Cycles (MWU-MEM)" seems to lack some theoretical rigor in terms of the asymptotic performance. E.g., one can't obtain large sample SEs for the new item parameter estimates since the initial calibration parameters are treated as fixed and known, and even if the parameters were fixed but still included in the ACOV computation there's no way these algorithms are guaranteed to be at some maximum-likelihood point in the parameter space. The calibration with the empirically updated prior weights is also a function of the number of quadrature points used since these aren't 'free' parameters (they cost Q - 1 degrees of freedom to estimate, which doesn't appear in the calibration results). I suppose one could do something like a bootstrap calibration to obtain better sampling variability estimates, or more efficiently some modification of a delta method, for example, but any method that doesn't give theoretically justifiable sampling variability estimates always puts me a little on edge....  Cheers.

Phil

messages.subject_clean: Estimating DIF for a multi-group multi-dimensional model w/highly correlated latent parameters
messages.body_plain:
Hi mirters,

I'm trying to estimate a multi-group multi-dimensional model w/highly correlated latent parameters. My model includes five indicators: three on one latent, two on another. I realize that this model is just barely identified, and that this sounds like a situation that calls for a unidimensional model. And I am interested in a unidimensional model, but I need to estimation both the uni and multi models. For the sake of this post, please trust that I have good reasons to test the two-factor model, so it's important for me to be able to properly estimate and parameterize.

Unsurprisingly, the multidimensional model has difficulty converging. I read on another post by Dr. Chalmers that I should try to use the method = "MHRM" argument, because the stochastic estimation procedure of MHRM makes it less susceptible to model failure in my situation. That worked: I was able to estimate the model, and run DIF tests on the items using the DIF() function in mirt!

Now here's the problem. All of the multidimensional DIF tests came back indicating DIF. But when I estimated a unidimensional model based on the same items using the EM estimator, the DIF tests came back indicating the items are non-DIF. And the difference between the DIF results for the two models was enormous - chi squared values for the uni model were roughly < 10 on 7 df, but for the multi dimensional model they were > 100. And here's the kicker: when I went back and re-estimated the unidimensional model using method = "MHRM" argument, I got the same results as the multidimensional model, indicating that the items are all DIF.

I should say I also have good reason to expect these items are probably non-DIF, because MI tests in the CFA framework (using the fixed-factor method) based on both the uni and multi models indicate that the models are invariant. That's data-driven evidence that the items might be invariant. It is imperfect evidence, but makes me skeptical that my items are all DIF

Take together, this set of results makes me think DIF results for the multidimensional model appear to be an artifact of the MHRM estimation, rather than being truly DIF (however, this statement assume that EM is globally more valid than MHRM). My primary question is, Is there a better way to estimate the multidimensional model to get appropriate DIF results? I am not fishing for a way to get non-DIF: if the items are DIF, then so be it. But right now I don't trust the results of the method = "MHRM" estimation technique.

Here is the code for the multidimensional model I'm trying to run, as well as a print out of the item parameters and DIF results:

### Two-factor model

# Two factor model syntax
dddTwoFactorIRTSyntax <- mirt.model(
'
symp = 1-3
tend = 4-5
COV = symp*tend
'
)

# Unrestrained two-factor multiple group model
ddd.model.multi.free <- mirt::multipleGroup(data = dddMirtData,
                                            model = dddTwoFactorIRTSyntax,
                                            itemtype = "graded",
                                            group = dddata$SexCode,
                                            method = "MHRM")

# Coefficients for the unrestrained two-factor multiple group model
coef(ddd.model.multi.free,
     simplify = TRUE)

# Constrain the model
ddd.constrained.multi.model <- mirt::multipleGroup(data = dddMirtData,
                                                   model = dddTwoFactorIRTSyntax,
                                                   itemtype = "graded",
                                                   group = dddata$SexCode,
                                                   invariance = c(colnames(dddMirtData),
                                                                  'free_means',
                                                                  'free_var'),
                                                   method = "MHRM")

# Constrain the parameters
ddd.constrained.multi.parameters <- coef(ddd.constrained.multi.model,
                                        simplify = TRUE)[[1]][[1]]

# First round of AOAA selection.
ddd.dif.drop.multi <- DIF(ddd.constrained.multi.model,
                          c('a1',
                            'a2',
                            'd1',
                            'd2',
                            'd3',
                            'd4',
                            'd5',
                            'd6'),
                          scheme = 'drop',
                          seq_stat = .05,
                          method = "MHRM")

## use the optional function to table the output
get.dif.items(f.data=ddd.dif.drop.multi,
              p.val=.05,
              parms=ddd.constrained.multi.parameters)

Hi Thomas,

It sounds like you've encountered a strange edge-case situation where even the ML estimation algorithms are at odds (which is not a great sign...). I checked that the procedure is performing as expected (see simulation code below), so I can only assume this is due to problematic data conditions with your dataset. Specifically, I can see unusually high slope parameters, indicating effectively step-functions (bad news), as well as extreme intercept locations, indicating very sparse cell counts (also bad news). The MHRM may be just masking things in this case as the MHRM really should only outperform the EM algorithm in cases when numerical integration becomes inaccurate (which, with two latent traits, shouldn't be the case), so it's likely the baseline model supplied to DIF() is rather far from a stable MLE location, and therefore relative comparisons based on likelihood criteria could in reference to an improper base model. I am speculating a little, but this seems the most likely case. HTH.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
Hi Yuanjin,

The p-value associated with G2 is a goodness-of-fit type detection value based on the complete cell frequencies (very unreliable as full-tables of counts are extremely sparse....hence why this is disabled by default). M2 is likely better since it is doing data collapsing to only the first and second moments to help removing sparceness. And yes, M2 is fine for an exploratory model.
